stem_md: The terms of an arithmetic sequence add to  $715$ . The first term of the sequence is increased by  $1$ , the second term is increased by  $3$ , the third term is increased by  $5$ , and in general, the  $k$ th term is increased by the  $k$ th odd positive integer. The terms of the new sequence add to  $836$ . Find the sum of the first, last, and middle terms of the original sequence.
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>Let the arithmetic sequence be  $a_1 + a_2 + a_3 + \dots + a_n = 715$ .

We also have  $(a_1+1) + (a_2 + 3) + (a_3 + 5) + (a_n+(2n-1)) = 836$ .

Notice that the first arithmetic sequence is in the second arithmetic sequence. We can rewrite the second arithmetic sequence as 
\[ (a_1 + a_2 + a_3 + \dots + a_n) + (1 + 3 + 5 + \dots + (2n-1))\]
Which is also  $715 + (1+3+5+\dots+(2n-1))=836$ .

Note that the sum  $(1+3+5+\dots+(2n-1))=n^2$ . Therefore we have  $n^2 = 836-715 = 121$ . We now have  $n=11$ .

Now we are looking for the sum of  $a_1+a_6+a_{11}$ . We know that  $a_6$  will be the average of  $a_1$  and  $a_{11}$ , so from that we know that  $a_1+a_{11} = 2a_6$ .

Now if we continue the average of  $a_2$  and  $a_{10}$  will also be  $a_6$  so the sum of  $a_2$  and  $a_{10}$  is  $2a_6$ .

If we continue this, we should see that the sum of  $a_1 + a_2 + a_3 + \dots + a_{11} = 735$  will just be equivalent to  $11a_6 = 735$ . 

Note that  $a_1+a_{11}+a_6 = 2a_6 + a_6 = 3a_6$ , so we can just multiply  $735$  by  $11a_6=735$  by  $\frac{3}{11}$  to get  $3a_6=715\left(\frac{3}{11}\right) = \boxed{195}$ .</details>

stem_md: Nine people sit down for dinner where there are three choices of meals. Three people order the beef meal, three order the chicken meal, and three order the fish meal. The waiter serves the nine meals in random order. Find the number of ways in which the waiter could serve the meal types to the nine people such that exactly one person receives the type of meal ordered by that person.
solution_md:
<details><summary>My solution during test</summary>Assume WLOG that this person that gets his correct order chooses beef (we multiply by 3 at the end to correct for this, and multiply by another 3 for which person gets it from the people that choose beef).  
We have orders of:  2B, 3C, 3F and to give:  2B, 3C, 3F.  For the people that order 2B, they can get one of the following:  (C/C, C/F, F/C, F/F)**Case 1:**  $C/C$  or  $F/F$ WLOG assume that it is  $C/C$  and multiply by 2 at end of case to account for getting  $F/F$ .  
Food orders:  3C, 3F
Food left to give:  2B, C, 3F

The people that ordered chicken must be given fish, because if they won't then the fish will go to a fish person, and we'll get two people with fish.
Then, we have the following:
Food orders:  3F
Food left to give:  2B, C

We have  $\binom{3}{1}=3$  ways to choose which person gets fish, and the total count for  $\binom{3}{1}*2=6$ .**Case 2:**  $C/F$  or  $F/C$ Again, WLOG assume that it is  $C/F$ , and multiply by  $2$ .  
We get:
Food left:  2B, 2C, 2F
Orders:  3C, 3F
For people who ordered chicken, we could have  $(2B/F)$  or  $(B/2F)$ .  The first case gives us  $2C, F$  to give to people who ordered fish, however, this would give us one person having fish, which would give us a total of  $2$  people getting the correct order, contradiction.  In the second case, we have  $\binom{3}{1}=3$  ways to choose who gets the beef.  Then, we get the following:
Food left:  B, 2C
Orders:  3F

We have  $\binom{3}{1}=1$  way to choose which person that ordered fish gets beef, and overall we get  $\binom{3}{1}*\binom{3}{1}=9$  ways for  $C/F$ .  Multiplying by  $2$  gives  $9*2=18$ .  

Adding case 1/case 2 gives  $6+18=24$ .  Times 9 from beginning give  $24*9=\boxed{216}$ .</details>

Nine people sit down for dinner where there are three choices of meals. Three people order the beef meal, three order the chicken meal, and three order the fish meal. The waiter serves the nine meals in random order. Find the number of ways in which the waiter could serve the meal types to the nine people such that exactly one person receives the type of meal ordered by that person.
SolutionWe will split it into cases: - Case 1: One of the people who ordered beef got the correct meal [list] - Case 1.1: The two people who got the other two beef meals both ordered fish - Case 1.2: The two people who got the other two beef meals ordered fish and chicken - Case 1.3: The two people who got the other two beef meals both ordered chicken[/list] Note that the corresponding Case 2 and Case 3 are equivalent, so we can multiply by three at the end. In Case 1, there are three ways to choose which person got the correct meal. In Case 1.1, there are $\dbinom32 = 3$ ways to choose which two people got the beef meals. Now we know that the three people who ordered chicken got fish meals, because there are no more beef meals. The remaining chicken meals go to the remaining people. Case 1.3 is equivalent to this In Case 1.2, there are $3 \cdot 3 = 9$ ways to choose which person who ordered fish and which person who ordered chicken got the beef meals. Now the remaining two people who ordered chicken must get fish meals, and the remaining two people who ordered fish must get chicken meals. There are then two ways to choose which one out of the remaining people who ordered beef gets the remaining chicken meal (and the last person gets the remaining fish meal) Therefore, we have a total of $3(3 \cdot 2 + 3 \cdot 3 \ cdot 2) = 72$ ways in Case 1, so we have $3 \cdot 72 = \boxed{216}$ ways in total.

stem_md: Butch and Sundance need to get out of Dodge. To travel as quickly as possible, each alternates walking and riding their only horse, Sparky, as follows. Butch begins walking as Sundance rides. When Sundance reaches the first of their hitching posts that are conveniently located at one-mile intervals along their route, he ties Sparky to the post and begins walking. When Butch reaches Sparky, he rides until he passes Sundance, then leaves Sparky at the next hitching post and resumes walking, and they continue in this manner. Sparky, Butch, and Sundance walk at 6, 4, and 2.5 miles per hour, respectively. The first time Butch and Sundance meet at a milepost, they are  $n$  miles from Dodge, and have been traveling for  $t$  minutes. Find  $n + t$ .
solution_md:
<details><summary>a good solution</summary>Sparky takes 10 minutes to walk a mile, Butch takes 15 minutes to walk a mile, and Sundance takes 24 minutes to walk a mile.

Now let  $B_i$  and  $S_i$  be the time it takes for Butch and Sundance to get to the  $i$ th mile marker, respectively. We can now make a recursion:

If  $B_i<S_i$ , then Butch gets to the  $i$ th mile marker before Sundance, so Butch walks the  $i+1$ st mile and Sundance rides the  $i+1$ st mile, so  $B_{i+1}=B_i+15$  and  $S_{i+1}+10$ .
If  $B_i>S_i$ , then  $B_{i+1}=B_i+10$  and  $S_{i+1}=S_i+24$  by the same reasoning.

Let  $a_i=B_i-S_i$ . We then have that:

If  $a_i>0$ ,  $a_{i+1}=a_i-14$ .
If  $a_i<0$ ,  $a_{i+1}=a_i+5$ .

It's not hard to see that the least  $i>0$  such that  $a_i=0$  is 19, and that there are 5  $i$  between 0 and 19 such that  $a_i>0$ . This shows that Butch rides Sparky for a total of 5 miles and Sundance rides Sparky for 14 miles, and it takes a total of  $5*10+14*15$  (or  $14*10+5*24$ ), or  $260$  minutes to travel 19 miles. This gives an answer of  $\boxed{279}$ .</details>
This is basically superpi's solution put into algebraic terms.

stem_md: Let  $B$  be the set of all binary integers that can be written using exactly 5 zeros and 8 ones where leading zeros are allowed. If all possible subtractions are performed in which one element of  $B$  is subtracted from another, find the number of times the answer 1 is obtained.
solution_md:
Let $B$ be the set of all binary integers that can be written using exactly 5 zeros and 8 ones where leading zeros are allowed. If all possible subtractions are performed in which one element of $B$ is subtracted from another, find the number of times the answer 1 is obtained.
SolutionThere are four possible endings to a binary number: $00$ , $01$ , $10$ , and $11$ . It is clear that the first 11 digits of two numbers in $B$ have to be the same in order to preserve the number of $0$ s and $1$ s, and to make the difference $0$ . Therefore, if two numbers in $B$ have a difference of $1$ , then their last two digits should also have a difference of $1$ . The only pair of digits in the possible endings that preserves the number of $0$ s and $1$ s and also has a difference of $1$ is $01$ and $10$ . Therefore, the problem is just making up the rest of the number, which can be done in $\dbinom{11}{4} = \boxed{330}$ .

Case 1: Integer ending in 1
Subtract 1 and you get a number ending in 0.

Case 2: Integer ending in 10
Subtract 1 and you get a number ending in 01.

Case 3: Integer ending in 100
Subtract 1 and you get a number ending in 011.

Case 4...n: Integer ending in 10...0
Subtract 1 and you get a number ending in 01...1

Only case 2 produces a valid result. The number of integers corresponding to case 2 are numbers beginning with 7 ones and 4 zeros in some order and ending in 10. So, the answer is C(11,7)=330.</details>

<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>consider the binary numbers  $a$  and  $b$  such that  $a,b\in{B}$ . we are given the requirement that they each have exactly 5 zeroes and 8 ones and also  $a-b=1\Leftrightarrow{a=b+1}$  (here we assumed WLOG that a>b).

This leaves us with pairs  $a,b$  such that  $b$  ends in  $01$ , and since leading zeroes are allowed, we have 4 zeroes and 7 ones left to place anywhere on 11 empty spaces, i.e.  ${{11}\choose{4}}=\boxed{330}$  such numbers  $b\in{B}$ .</details>

**Solution:** Notice that, for a possible subtraction of two elements of  $B$  to result in  $1$ , one element has to end in  $0$  and the other in  $1$ . stem_md: The complex numbers  $z$  and  $w$  satisfy  $z^{13} = w$ ,  $w^{11} = z$ , and the imaginary part of  $z$  is  $\sin\left(\frac{m\pi}n\right)$  for relatively prime positive integers  $m$  and  $n$  with  $m < n$ . Find  $n$ .
solution_md:
Replace  $w$  in the second equation with  $z^{13}$ . 

Then we have that  $z^{143} = z$ . Dividing both sides by  $z$  gives us  $z^{142} = z$ . 

Finding the real and imaginary parts of z in terms of  $sin$  and  $cos$  are trivial with the roots of unity.

By roots of unity, the solutions to  $z^{n} = 1$  are in the form of  $\operatorname{cis}\left(\frac{2\pi k}n\right)$ .

Thus, plugging in  $142$  for  $n$  gives us  $\operatorname{cis}\left(\frac{\pi k}{71}\right)$ .  $\operatorname{Cis}\left(\frac{\pi k}{71}\right)$  is equivalent to  $\cos \left(\frac{\pi k}{71}\right) + i\sin \left(\frac{\pi k}{71} \right)$ . 

Finally, the imaginary part is  $\sin \left(\frac{\pi k}{71} \right)$ .

Since we are looking only for  $n$ , our answer is  $\boxed{071}$ .

It's important to note that  $71$  is prime, so  $n$  has to be  $71$ .

Thus  $w^{142}=z^{142}=1$ , so each is of the form  $sin(2*pi*k/142)$  where  $k$  is a positive integer between  $0$  and  $141$  inclusive.  This simplifies to  $sin(pi*k/71)$ , and  $071$  is prime, so it is the only possible denominator, and thus is the answer.</details>

solution_md: **Solution:** Let the center initially have  $n$  coins. Then, after the center circle gives away all its coins, it gains all  $n$  back through its five direct neighbors. (Call the direct neighbors of the center circle *semi-center*.) Hence, all semi-center circles give  $\frac{n}{5}$  coins to its neighbors. Since those circles have three neighbors, they start out with  $\frac{3n}{5}$  coins. (Call the direct neighbors of the semi-center circles *semi-outer*.) Notice that, since one of the semi-center circles starts out, and therefore, must end with  $\frac{3n}{5}$  coins, and the center circle gives  $\frac{n}{5}$  coins, each semi-outer circle gives  $\frac{n}{5}$  to each of its two semi-center neighbors, and, therefore, gives that amount to the two of its mostouter neighbor circles as well. Hence, the semi-outer circles start with  $\frac{4n}{5}$  coins. Furthermore, this means that the outermost circles give  $\frac{n}{5}$  coins to the semi-outer circles (since the semi-center circles give that many coins to their neighbors). Since the outermost circles have four neighbors, they start out with  $\frac{4n}{5}$  coins. In total, all the circles start out with  $n + 5\frac{3n}{5} + 5\frac{4n}{5} + 5\frac{4n}{5} = 12n$  coins. Finally, we get that  $12n = 3360 \Rightarrow n = \boxed{280}$ .

stem_md: Let  $\mathcal{S}$  be the set of all perfect squares whose rightmost three digits in base  $10$  are  $256$ . Let  $\mathcal{T}$  be the set of all numbers of the form  $\frac{x-256}{1000}$ , where  $x$  is in  $\mathcal{S}$ . In other words,  $\mathcal{T}$  is the set of numbers that result when the last three digits of each number in  $\mathcal{S}$  are truncated. Find the remainder when the tenth smallest element of  $\mathcal{T}$  is divided by  $1000$ .
solution_md:
<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>We don't really need to think about the set  $\mathcal{T}$ ; it is only used in the problem statement to make the actual question being asked easier to state.

All numbers  $x^2$  in  $\mathcal{S}$  satisfy  $x^2 - 16^2 \equiv 0 \pmod {1000}$ , so  $(x + 16)(x - 16) \equiv 0 \pmod {1000}$ . Obviously,  $x \equiv \pm 16 \pmod {1000}$  works. Are there any other solutions?

Somehow we have to fit all the factors of 1000 into  $(x+16) * (x-16)$ , which includes three 5s and three 2s. Since  $x + 16$  and  $x - 16$  differ by 32, obviously all three factors of 5 must be in one of them. Also, if that number is not divisible by 4, then the second one will not be either, and not enough factors of two will be present; so one of  $x \pm 16$  must have three factors of 5 and two factors of 2. Thus, we see all solutions are of the form  $x \equiv 0 \pm 16$  or  $x \equiv 500 \pm 16 \pmod {1000}$ . Listing out possible values of  $x$ : $16, 500 \pm 16, 1000 \pm 16, 1500 \pm 16, 2000 \pm 16, 2500 \pm 16$ ...

With  $x = 2500 - 16$  being the 10th solution.  $(2500-16)^2 = 2500^2 - 180000 + 256 = 6250000 - 180000 + 256 = 6170256$ , and so the answer is  $\boxed{170}$ .</details>

stem_md: Let  $x$ ,  $y$ , and  $z$  be positive real numbers that satisfy \[ 2\log_x(2y) = 2\log_{2x}(4z) = \log_{2x^4}(8yz) \neq 0. \] The value of  $xy^5z$  can be expressed in the form  $\frac{1}{2^{p/q}}$ , where  $p$  and  $q$  are relatively prime integers.  Find  $p+q$ .
solution_md: Let  $a=\log_2x$ ,  $b=\log_2y$ ,  $c=\log_2z$ . With  $\log/\exp$  rules we rewrite the equations as:  $$ \frac{2b+2}a=\frac{2c+4}{a+1}=\frac{b+c+3}{4a+1} $$  and we want to find  $a+5b+c=-\frac pq$ . Recall that  $\frac pq=\frac rs=t$  implies  $t=\frac{p+r}{q+s}$ , so applying this here gives:  $$ \frac{2b+2c+6}{2a+1}=\frac{b+c+3}{4a+1}\Rightarrow a=-\frac16. $$  Then the equations rewrite as:  $$ -\frac13b-\frac13=\frac{12}5c+\frac{24}5=3b+3c+9 $$  or  $$ -5b-5=36c+72=45b+45c+135. $$  The second equality implies  $45b+45c+135=36c+72$ , or  $45b+9c+63=0$ , or  $5b+c+7=0$ . Then  $a+5b+c=-\frac16-7=-\frac{43}6$ , so the answer is  $43+6=\boxed{049}$ .

stem_md: Let  $\triangle ABC$  be a right triangle with right angle at  $C$ . Let  $D$  and  $E$  be points on  $\overline{AB}$  with  $D$  between  $A$  and  $E$  such that  $\overline{CD}$  and  $\overline{CE}$  trisect  $\angle C$ .  If  $\frac{DE}{BE} = \frac{8}{15}$ , then  $\tan B$  can be written as  $\frac{m\sqrt{p}}{n}$ , where  $m$  and  $n$  are relatively prime positive integers, and  $p$  is a positive integer not divisible by the square of any prime.  Find  $m+n+p$ .
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>See the following diagram by djmathman:  
[asy]
size(150);
defaultpen(linewidth(0.8));
pair A=(9/2,0),B=(0,6),C=(0,0), x=dir(30)*12, y=dir(60)*12,D=extension(A,B,C,x),E=extension(A,B,C,y);
draw(A--B--C--cycle^^D--C--E);
label(" $B$ ",A,SE);
label(" $A$ ",B,NW);
label(" $C$ ",C,SW);
label(" $E$ ",D,NE);
label(" $D$ ",E,NE);
draw(rightanglemark(A,C,B));

[/asy]
Note that  $\angle ACD=\angle DCE=\angle ECB=30^\circ$ .

From the law of sines: $\frac{\sin(30^\circ)}{8x}=\frac{\sin(\angle CDE)}{CE}$  $\frac{\sin(30^\circ)}{15x}=\frac{\sin(\angle DBC)}{CE}$ Hence  $8x\sin(\angle CDE)=15x\sin(\angle DBC)=\sin(30^\circ)CE$  or  $8\sin(\angle CDE)=15\sin(\angle DBC)$ .

Note that  $\angle CDE+\angle DBC=120^\circ$  from  $\triangle CDB$  having  $\angle DCB=60^\circ$ .   Hence, we get  $\angle CDE=120^\circ-\angle DBC$ .

Substitute this in to give us  $8\sin(120^\circ-\angle DBC)=15\sin(\angle DBC)$ .  This gives us  $8*(\sin(120^\circ)\cos(\angle DBC)-\cos(120^\circ)\sin(\angle DBC))=15\sin(\angle DBC)$ .  This implies that  $4\sqrt3\cos(\angle DBC)+4\sin(\angle DBC)=15\sin(\angle DBC)$  which gives us: $ 4\sqrt3\cos(\angle DBC)=11\sin(\angle DBC)\implies \frac{\sin(\angle DBC)}{\cos(\angle DBC)}=\frac{4\sqrt3}{11}$  which is the same as  $\tan(\angle DBC)$  or  $\tan(B)$ .  This implies that we get an answer of  $4+3+11=\boxed{18}$ .</details>
P.S.  @trigonometry456103:  This problem does involve a bash aspect, although it isn't really a hard problem.  I would say that this problem is definitely not easier than, say problem 1 or problem 6, both of which took like a minute to do.  I would probably say this problem was around the fourth-fifth hardest on the test.

stem_md: Three concentric circles have radii  $3$ ,  $4$ , and  $5$ .  An equilateral triangle with one vertex on each circle has side length  $s$ .  The largest possible area of the triangle can be written as  $a+\frac{b}{c}\sqrt{d}$ , where  $a,b,c$  and  $d$  are positive integers,  $b$  and  $c$  are relatively prime, and  $d$  is not divisible by the square of any prime.  Find  $a+b+c+d$ .
solution_md: The red part could use some rigor. Assume $a=3,$ then we have $|b|=4,|c|=5,$ and by EGMO Lemma 6.28 our triangle is equilateral iff $3^2+b^2+c^2=3(b+c)+bc.$ This solves using the quadratic formula as $$ b^2-b(c+3)+c^2-3c+9=0 $$ $$ 2b=3+c \pm \sqrt{(c+3)-4(c^2-3c+9)}=3+c \pm i\sqrt{3}(c-3). $$ Assume it's the positive case, and solving for $c$ yields $c=\frac{2b-3+3i\sqrt{3}}{1+i\sqrt{3}}.$ Taking the magnitude of both sides, $$ 5=|c|=\left|\frac{2b-3+3i\sqrt{3}}{1+i\sqrt{3}}\right|=\frac{|2b-3+3i\sqrt{3}|}{|1+i\sqrt{3}|} $$ thus $10=|2b-3+3i\sqrt{3}|.$ Let $b=p+qi$ for reals $p,q,$ then $|b|=4$ is equivalent to $$ p^2+q^2=16\implies q=-\sqrt{16-p^2} $$ where we assume the negative case to maximize area (we set $a=3$ ). We also derive $$ 10=|2p-3+i(2q+3\sqrt{3})| $$ which yields $$ (2p-3)^2+(2q+3\sqrt{3})^2=100. $$ Substituting, $$ (2p-3)^2+(2(-\sqrt{16-p^2})+3\sqrt{3})^2=100 $$ $$ 4p^2-12p-91=-(2\sqrt{16-p^2}-3\sqrt{3})^2 $$ $$ 4p^2-12p-91=-4(16-p^2)+12\sqrt{3}\sqrt{16-p^2}-27 $$ And somehow, magically, this cancels to $$ \cancel{4p^2}-12p\cancel{-91}=\cancel{-64}+\cancel{4p^2}+12\sqrt{48-3p^2}\cancel{-27} $$ $$ -p=\sqrt{48-3p^2} \implies p=-2\sqrt{3}. $$ The area of our triangle can be expressed as $\tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}|b-3|^2,$ and note that $$ |b-3|^2=(b-3)(\overline{b}-3)=b\overline{b}-3(b+\overline{b})+9, $$ and since $16=|b|^2=b\overline{b},$ our answer is equivalent to $$ \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}(25-3(b+\overline{b}))=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}(25-6p)=\boxed{9+\frac{25\sqrt{3}}{4}}. $$

Denote  $\angle OCA = 30^\circ - \theta$ ,  $\angle OCB = 30^\circ + \theta$ . By Law of Cosines on  $\triangle AOC$  and  $\triangle BOC$  we obtain the relations
\[3^2 = 5^2 + x^2 - 10x \cos(30^\circ - \theta)\]
\[4^2 = 5^2 + x^2 - 10x \cos(30^\circ + \theta).\]
Adding the equations and simplifying we have
\[-25 = 2x^2 - 10x \sqrt{3} \cos(\theta) \implies \cos(\theta) = \dfrac{2x^2 + 25}{10x \sqrt{3}} \]
whereas subtracting the first equation from the second yields
\[7 = 10x \sin(\theta) \implies \sin(\theta) = \dfrac{7}{10x}.\]
Allow  $y = x^2$ , adding the squares of the last two equations gives us
\[\dfrac{(2x^2 + 25)^2}{300x^2} + \dfrac{49}{100x^2} = 1 \implies y^2 - 25y + 193 = 0\]
upon simplifying, which yields the solutions  $y = 25 - 12 \sqrt{3}, 25 + 12 \sqrt{3}$ . Now  $x = \sqrt{y} = \sqrt{25 - 12 \sqrt{3}} < 5$ , but  $O$  lies in  $ABC$ , contradiction. So  $y = 25 + 12 \sqrt{3} \implies[ABC] = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4} y = \dfrac{36 + 25 \sqrt{3}}{4}$ .

Denote the equilateral triangle as  $\triangle ABC$ . Rephrase the condition as follows: There exists a point  $P$  such that  $PA=3$ ,  $PB=4$ , and  $PC=5$ . Note that for an equilateral triangle  $\triangle ABC$  with side length  $s$  and a point  $P$  satisfying  $PA=a$ ,  $PB=b$ , and  $PC=c$ , we have

\[3(a^4+b^4+c^4+s^4) = (a^2+b^2+c^2+s^2)^2.\]

Plugging in the values we have yields  $s^2 = 25 \pm 12\sqrt{3}$ , but we obviously want the larger case. Then, 

\[[ABC] = s^2 \cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4} = \boxed{\frac{36+25\sqrt{3}}{4}}.\]

stem_md: Complex numbers  $a$ ,  $b$  and  $c$  are the zeros of a polynomial  $P(z) = z^3+qz+r$ , and  $|a|^2+|b|^2+|c|^2=250$ .  The points corresponding to  $a$ ,  $b$ , and  $c$  in the complex plane are the vertices of a right triangle with hypotenuse  $h$ .  Find  $h^2$ .
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>Firstly, since the coefficient of  $z^2$  is  $0$  in  $P(z),$  it follows that  $a+b+c=0.$  Therefore, we have  $\tfrac{a+b+c}{3}=0$  as well which means that the centroid of the right triangle must be at the origin. Therefore, it follows that  $|a|, |b|,$  and  $|c|$  are  $\tfrac{2}{3}$  of the lengths of the medians of the triangle, which implies that the sum of the squares of the medians is   $$ 250\cdot\frac{9}{4} = \frac{1125}{2}. $$   On the other hand, if we let the legs of the triangle have lengths  $x$  and  $y,$  then the sum of the squares of the medians is also
\begin{align*}
    x^2+\left(\frac{y}{2}\right)^2+\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)^2+y^2+\left(\frac{h}{2}\right)^2 &= x^2+\frac{y^2}{4}+\frac{x^2}{4}+y^2+\frac{h^2}{4} 
    &= \frac{5}{4}(x^2+y^2)+\frac{h^2}{2} 
    &= \frac{5h^2}{4}+\frac{h^2}{4} 
    &= \frac{3h^2}{2}.
\end{align*}
Hence, we have
\begin{align*}
    \frac{1125}{2} = \frac{3h^2}{2} &\implies h^2=\boxed{375}.
\end{align*} $\square$</details>

Multiplying each  $a,b,c$  by a complex number with magnitude 1 (effectively rotating  $a,b,c$ ) preserves these conditions, so we may assume without loss of generality that the two legs are parallel to the axes. Since the conditions are symmetric in  $a,b,c$ , we may also suppose without loss of generality that  $c$  corresponds to the right angle, the leg joining  $a$  and  $c$  is parallel to the real axis, and the leg joining  $b$  and  $c$  is parallel to the imaginary axis. Thus, we may set  $c=x+yi$ ,  $a = x+yi+r$ , and  $b = x+yi + si$  for some reals  $x,y,r,s$ . 

Since  $a+b+c=0$ , we have  $(3x + r) + i(3y + s) = 0$ , whence  $r=-3x$  and  $s=-3y$ . Thus,  $a = -2x + iy$  and  $b = x - 2yi$ , so 
\[ |a|^2 + |b|^2 + |c|^2 = (2x)^2 + y^2 + x^2 + (2y)^2 + x^2 + y^2 = 250 \implies 6(x^2+y^2) = 250. \]
The length  $h$  is  $|a-b| = |r-is| = \sqrt{r^2 + s^2} = \sqrt{9(x^2 + y^2)}$ , so
\[ h^2 = 9(x^2 + y^2) = \frac{3}{2} \cdot 6(x^2+y^2) = \frac{3}{2} \cdot 250 = \boxed{375}. \]</details>

<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>I didn't take the AIME, but I did this and it appears that most of the solutions here are algebraic; here's a more geometric one.

Since the sum of the roots is  $0$ , it follows that the origin  $0+0i$  is the centroid of said triangle. Then the segment from the origin to a root is the distance from the centroid to a vertex. The sum of the squares of these segments is  $250$ , which means that the sum of the squares of the segments from the centroid to each vertex is  $250$ . But since each segment is  $\frac{2}{3}$  of the median, this is just  $\frac{4}{9}$  the sum of the squares of the medians. But the sum of the squares of the medians is  $\frac{3}{4}$  the sum of the squares of the sides, which is just twice the square of the hypotenuse.

So we have  $250 = \frac{4}{9}\cdot \frac{3}{4} \cdot 2c^2 = \frac{2}{3}c^2 \implies c^2 = \frac{250 \cdot 3}{2} = \boxed{375}$ .</details>

The magnitudes of  $a$ ,  $b$ , and  $c$  are just  $\frac{2}{3}$  of the medians because the origin, or the centroid in this case, cuts the median in a ratio of  $2:1$ . Similarly,  $|c|^2=\frac{4}{9}\cdot(x^2+(\frac{y}{2})^2)=\frac{4x^2}{9}+\frac{y^2}{9}$ . The median from  $b$  is just half the hypotenuse because the hypotenuse of any right triangle is just half the hypotenuse. So,  $|b|^2=\frac{4}{9}\cdot\frac{x^2+y^2}{4}=\frac{x^2}{9}+\frac{y^2}{9}$ . Hence,  $|a|^2+|b|^2+|c|^2=\frac{6x^2+6y^2}{9}=\frac{2x^2+2y^2}{3}=250$ . Expanding  $(\overline a+\overline b+\overline c)(a+b+c)$  yields  $a\overline a+b\overline b+c\overline c+\sum_{sym}a\overline b=250+\sum_{sym}a\overline b=0$ , or  $\sum_{sym}a\overline b=-250$ . The condition that states that  $a, b, c$  form a right triangle, so we have another equation  $|b-c|^2+|c-a|^2=|a-b|^2$ , or  $(a\overline a+b\overline b+c\overline c)+c\overline c-(b\overline c+\overline b c+c\overline a+\overline c a)=(a\overline a+b\overline b)-(a\overline b+\overline a b)$ , or  $2c\overline c+250+2a\overline b+2\overline a b=0$ . stem_md:
There are  $n$  mathematicians seated around a circular table with  $n$  seats numbered  $1,2,3,\cdots,n$  in clockwise order.  After a break they again sit around the table.   The mathematicians note that there is a positive integer  $a$  such that

    (1) for each  $k$ , the mathematician who was seated in seat  $k$  before the break is seated in seat  $ka$  after the break (where seat  $i+n$  is seat  $i$ );
    (2) for every pair of mathematicians, the number of mathematicians sitting between them after the break, counting in both the clockwise and the counterclockwise directions, is different from either of the number of mathematicians sitting between them before the break.

Find the number of possible values of  $n$  with  $1<n<1000$ .
solution_md:
Yay finally a number theory #15.

<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>For a specific  $a$ , the first condition holds iff no two mathematicians sit in the same seat after the break, in other words,  $ka\neq \ell a\pmod n$  for any  $k,\ell\in\{1,2,\dots,n\}$ , or  $(k-\ell)a\neq 0\pmod n$  for any  $k,\ell\in\{1,2,\dots,n\}$  with  $k\neq \ell$ . Since  $k-\ell$  obviously ranges over all  numbers in  $\{1,2,\dots,n-1\}$  mod n, this means that  $a$  must be relatively prime to  $n$  since otherwise there is a positive integer  $1<b<n$  such that  $n\mid ab$ .

The second condition implies that  $k-\ell\neq \pm(ka-\ell a)\pmod n$  for any  $k,\ell\in\{1,2,\dots,n\}$ , or  $(a\pm 1)(k-\ell)\neq 0\pmod n$ . This implies that both  $a-1$  and  $a+1$  must be relatively prime to  $n$ .

Thus  $n$  satisfies the problem iff there exists a positive integer  $a$  such that  $a-1,a,a+1$  are all coprime to  $n$ .
If  $2\mid n$  or  $3\mid n$  then by the Pigeonhole principle, one of  $a-1,a,a+1$  is a multiple of 2 and one of them is a multiple of 3, violating the respective condition. Conversely, if all of the prime factors of  $n$  are at least 5, then  $a=2$  or  $a=3$  works.

The answer is the number of positive integers in  $\{2,3,\dots,999\}$  not divisible by 2 or 3, which is  $998-499-333+166=\boxed{332}$ .</details>

This is simply the cross product of MD and MN: $\left| \begin{matrix} \hat{\imath} & \hat{\jmath} & \hat{k}  \frac{-1}{2} & 1 & 0  \frac{1}{2} & 1 & \frac{1}{2} \end{matrix} \right| = \frac{1}{2} \hat{\imath} + \frac{1}{4} \hat{\jmath} - \hat{k}$ So the normal is < $\frac{1}{2}$ , $\frac{1}{4}$ , $-1$ >. Since the origin M lies in the plane, the equation of the plane is therefore: $z = \frac{1}{2} x + \frac{1}{4} y$ .

Some rudimentary knowledge of multivariable calculus allows you to easily determine the limits of integration and calculate the volume with a triple integral: $\int_0^1 \int_{\frac{-1}{2} y}^{1/2} \int_0^{\frac{1}{2} x + \frac{1}{4} y} dzdxdy = \frac{7}{48}$ .

This is the volume of the smaller solid, but we want the volume of the larger solid: $1 - \frac{7}{48} = \frac{41}{48}$ . $41+48 = \boxed{089}$ .</details>

$p$  and  $q$  are to be RELATIVELY prime.  That is to say, they are to have no common positive integer factors other than  $1$ . solution_md:
Two geometric sequences $ a_1,a_2,a_3,\ldots$ and $b_1,b_2,b_3\ldots $ have the same common ratio, with $a_1=27$ , $b_1=99$ , and $a_{15}=b_{11}$ . Find $a_9.$

stem_md: Find the number of ordered pairs of positive integer solutions  $(m,n)$  to the equation  $20m+12n=2012.$
solution_md:
<details><summary>Units digits sol</summary>We have  $20m+12n=2012.$  Instead of dividing it, we notice that  $20m$  can only have a units digit of  $0,$  no matter what  $m$  is. So, that means the units digit of  $12n$  must be  $2.$ We see the first 10 multiples of 12: 12, 24, 36, 48, 60, 72, 84, 96, 108, 120. Seeing this, we note that  $12n$ 's units digit can only be 2 if  $n = 1 (mod 5)$  as the pattern will hold

Knowing floor(2012/12)=167, we see n = {1, 6, 11, ... 161, 166} = {0, 5, 10, ... 160, 165} = {0, 1, 2, ... 32, 33} and there are 34 items in that list, so the answer is  $\boxed{34}.$</details>

stem_md: At a certain university, the division of mathematical sciences consists of the departments of mathematics, statistics, and computer science. There are two male and two female professors in each department. A committee of six professors is to contain three men and three women and must also contain two professors from each of the three departments. Find the number of possible comittees that can be formed subject to these requirements.
solution_md:
We take cases.

Case 1: One male and one female for each department.

There are  $4$  ways to pick a pair of one male and one female for one department, so the amount of ways is  $4^3 = 64$ .

Case 2: Two male from one department, two female from another department, and one male one female from the final department. 

The amount of ways to pick two male from one department and two females from another is  $1$ , and the amount of ways to pick one male one female is  $4$ , for  $1 \cdot 1 \cdot 4$  ways. However, since these are not all the same now, we need to account for arranging the departments, meaning that we must multiply by  $3! = 6 \implies 4 \cdot 6 = 24$  ways. Summing gives  $\boxed{88}$ .
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/AoPS Yearly Contest Collections/2012 Contests/2012 AIME Problems/472276.json

There are 6 ways to choose which departments have double-men and double-women, and 4 ways to choose the people in the man-woman department, giving  $6\times 4=24$  ways.

Solution**Case 1: One male professor and one female professor are chosen from each department for the committee** In each department, there are two ways to choose the male professor, and two ways to choose the female professor, so the total number of committees in this case is $(2 \cdot 2)^3 = 64$ **Case 2: One department sends two men, one department sends two women, and one department sends a man and a woman for the committee** There are three ways to choose which department sends the two men, and they have one way to do so. There are two ways to then choose which department sends the two women, and that department also has one way to do so. The remaining department has two ways to choose which male professor to send and two ways to choose which female professor to send, so there are $3 \cdot 2 \cdot 4 = 24$ ways in total In total, we have $64$ committees from Case 1, and $24$ committees from Case 2 $, so our answer is $ 64 + 24 = \boxed{088}$.

stem_md: In a group of nine people each person shakes hands with exactly two of the other people from the group. Let N be the number of ways this handshaking can occur. Consider two handshaking arrangements different if and only if at least two people who shake hands under one arrangement do not shake hands under the other arrangement. Find the remainder when N is divided by 1000.

recursion solLet $f_N$ be the number of ways a group of $N$ people can shake hands with exactly two of the other people from the group, where $N \ge 3$ . We can easily find that $f_3=1$ . Continuing on, we will label the people as $A$ , $B$ , $C$ ,... corresponding with $N$ . $f_4$ : There are $\dbinom{3}{2}=3$ possible ways for person $A$ to shake hands with two others (WLOG assume $A$ shakes hands with $B$ and $C$ ), and there is only one possible outcome thereon ( $B$ and $C$ both shakes hands with $D$ ). Therefore, we can conclude that $f_4=3$ $f_5$ : There are $\dbinom{4}{2}=6$ possible ways for person $A$ to shake hands with two others (WLOG assume they are $B$ and $C$ ). Then, $B$ and $C$ must also shake hands with the remaining two people ( $2$ ways), and those last $2$ people must shake hands with each other ( $1$ way). Therefore, $f_5=\dbinom{4}{2}\ast(2)\ast(1)=12$ $f_6$ : There are $\dbinom{5}{2}=10$ possible ways for person $A$ to shake hands with two others (WLOG assume they are $B$ and $C$ ). However, $B$ and $C$ shake hands with each other, then there are $f_3$ ways for the rest of the people to shake hands. If $B$ and $C$ shake hands with two others out of the three remaining people (3 $\ast$ 2 ways), those $2$ people must shake hands with the last person ( $1$ way). Therefore, $f_5=\dbinom{5}{2}\ast(f_3)+3\ast(2)\ast(1)=70$ Now we have enough information to find $f_9$ $f_9$ : There are $\dbinom{8}{2}=28$ possible ways for person $A$ to shake hands with two others (WLOG assume they are $B$ and $C$ ). Case 1: $B$ and $C$ shake hands with each other There are $f_6$ ways for $D$ , $E$ , $F$ , $G$ , $H$ , and $I$ to shake hands Case 2: $B$ and $C$ shake hands with one of the others out of the $6$ remaining people ( $6$ ways) There are $f_5$ ways for $E$ , $F$ , $G$ , $H$ , and $I$ to shake hands Case 3: If $B$ and $C$ shake hands with two different people (there are 6 $\ast$ 5 ways to choose the people but WLOG assume they are $D$ and $E$ ). Calculations of Case 3 are in its subcases. Subcase 3.1: $D$ and $E$ shake hands with each other There are $f_4$ ways for $F$ , $G$ , $H$ , and $I$ to shake hands Subcase 3.2: $D$ and $E$ each shake hands with one other person (there are $4$ ways to choose the person, WLOG let that be $F$ ) There are $f_3$ ways for $G$ , $H$ , and $I$ to shake hands Subcase 3.3: $D$ and $E$ each shake hands with two different people (there are 4 $\ast$ 3 ways, WLOG let that be $F$ and $G$ ) There are $2\ast1$ ways for $F$ and $G$ to then shake hands with $H$ and $I$ , and $H$ and $I$ will shake hands with each other. We have \begin{align*} 28(f_6+6\ast(f_5)+6\ast(5)\ast(f_4)+4\ast(f_3)+4\ast(3)\ast(2)\ast(1) &= 28(70+6\ast(12)+6\ast(5)\ast(3+4\ast(1)+4\ast(3)\ast(2)\ast(1) &= 30016 \end{align*} which gives us the answer of $\boxed{016}$

stem_md: For a positive integer  $p$ , define the positive integer  $n$  to be  $p$ -safe if  $n$  differs in absolute value by more than  $2$  from all multiples of  $p$ . For example, the set of  $10$ -safe numbers is  $\{3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17,23, \ldots \}$ . Find the number of positive integers less than or equal to  $10,000$  which are simultaneously  $7$ -safe,  $11$ -safe, and  $13$ -safe.·
solution_md:
For a positive integer $p$ , define the positive integer $n$ to be $p$ -safe if $n$ differs in absolute value by more than $2$ from all multiples of $p$ . For example, the set of $10$ -safe numbers is { ${3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17,23, ... }$ }. Find the number of positive integers less than or equal to $10,000$ which are simultaneously $7$ -safe, $11$ -safe, and $13$ -safe.·
SolutionFor a number $a$ to be 7, 11, and 13 safe, it must be - $a \equiv 3, 4 \pmod{7}$ - $a \equiv 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 \pmod{11}$ - $a \equiv 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 \pmod{13}$ By the Chinese Remainder theorem, there is only one solution every $1001$ numbers for each combination of residues. Therefore, there are $2 * 6 * 8 = 96$ 7-safe, 11-safe, and 13-safe positive integers less than or equal to $1001$ . Multiplying this by 10 gives that there are $960$ numbers of the condition less than 10010. Now notice that since $7 \cdot 11 \cdot 13 | 10010$ , 10007, 10006 are 7-safe, 11-safe, and 13-safe. The numbers 10005-10001 aren't 7-safe, so we only need to subtract out $10007$ and $10006$ , to obtain a final answer of $\boxed{958}$

stem_md: Ana, Bob, and Cao bike at constant rates of  $8.6$  meters per second,  $6.2$  meters per second, and  $5$  meters per second, respectively. They all begin biking at the same time from the northeast corner of a rectangular field whose longer side runs due west. Ana starts biking along the edge of the field, initially heading west, Bob starts biking along the edge of the field, initially heading south, and Cao bikes in a straight line across the field to a point D on the south edge of the field. Cao arrives at point D at the same time that Ana and Bob arrive at D for the first time. The ratio of the field's length to the field's width to the distance from point D to the southeast corner of the field can be represented as  $p : q : r$ , where  $p$ ,  $q$ , and  $r$  are positive integers with p and q relatively prime. Find  $p + q + r$ .
solution_md:
It is easier to set time to be a constant, like  $t=5$  to get rid of the decimals.  It makes the equations a lot easier to deal with as you don't have to set the nasty square root to another variable.

Let  $l,w,x$  be the length, width, and distance to the southeast corner from  $D$ .  We have, from  $d=rt$  with  $t=5$ , 
\begin{align} 2l+w-x=43 w+x=31 \sqrt{w^2+x^2}=25.\end{align}  Then, we can solve by squaring equation 2 and comparing with equation 3 to get  $wx=168$  and substitute  $w=\frac{168}{x}$  back into equation 2 to get  $x=24, w=7$  (the other case doesn't work as the width is longer than the length when substituted into equation 1) and using equation 1, we get  $l=30$  so our answer is  $\boxed{061}$ .

Since distance is proportional to speed when time is equal,  $AE+ED=31x$ , and  $AB+BC+CD=43$ . Then  $CD=6$ . By the Pythagorean Theorem,  $AE^2+ED^2=AD^2=625x^2$ . Solving for AE and ED, we get that they are  $24x$  and  $7x$  in some order. Because the longer side goes due west,  $24x$  must be DE and  $7x$  must be  $AE$ . Thus our desired ratio is  $30x:7x:24x=30:7:24$ , and our answer is  $\fbox{061}$ .</details>

Since $\ell>w$ , we have: \[ \ell:w:x = 60:14:48 = 30:7:24, \] so our answer is $\fbox{061}$ .

Let $z = a + bi$ be the complex number with $|z| = 5$ and $b > 0$ such that the distance between $(1 + 2i)z^3$ and $z^5$ is maximized, and let $z^4 = c + di$ . Find $c+d$ .
SolutionWe want to maximize $|z^5 - z^3(1+2i)| = 125|z^2 - (1+2i)|$ , so $z^2$ is the point with maximum distance from $(1,2)$ , while also on the circle $a^2 + b^2 = 625$ , because $|z^2| = 25$ [asy] import graph; size(200); Label f; f.p=fontsize(6); xaxis(" $x$ ",-26,26,Ticks(f, 5.0,5)); yaxis(" $y$ ",-26,26,Ticks(f, 5.0,5)); draw(Circle((0,0),25)); dot((-11.18034, -22.36068)); dot((1, 2)); draw((1, 2)--(-11.18034, -22.36068)); [/asy] We can find this point by solving $a^2 + b^2 = 625$ and $b = 2a$ , so $5a^2 = 625$ , so $(a,b) = (\pm 5\sqrt{5}, \pm 10\sqrt{5})$ , but we clearly want the negative one, so our complex number $z^2$ is $-5\sqrt{5} - 10\sqrt{5}i$ , so $z^4 = 5(\sqrt{5} + 2\sqrt{5}i)^2 = 25(-15 + 20i)$ , so our answer is $25(-15 + 20) = \boxed{125}$

By the triangle inequality,  $|z^2-(1+2i)| \le |z^2|+|1+2i|=25+\sqrt{5}$ . The equality case is achievable when  $z^2=-5\sqrt{5}-10\sqrt{5}i$ , so  $z^4=-375+500i$ , giving an answer of  $\fbox{125}$ .</details>

<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>Let  $z=e^{ix}$ . Then,  $(1+2i)z^3=e^{i(3x+y)}$  $z^5=e^{i5x}$ Notice that the maximal distance occurs when the arguments of each complex number is the reflection across the origin. Thus, $-e^{i(3x+y)}=e^{i5x}$  $-e^{iy}=e^{i2x}$ Notice that  $z^4=625e^{i4x}=625(-e^{iy})^2=625(1+2i)^2=625(\dfrac{-3+4i}{5})=500i-375$ Thus, the answer is  $500-375=125$ .</details>

stem_md: Let  $S$  be the increasing sequence of positive integers whose binary representation has exactly  $8$  ones. Let  $N$  be the  $1000^{th}$  number in  $S$ . Find the remainder when  $N$  is divided by  $1000$ .
solution_md:
Let $S$ be the increasing sequence of positive integers whose binary representation has exactly $8$ ones. Let $N$ be the $1000^{th}$ number in $S$ . Find the remainder when $N$ is divided by $1000$ .
SolutionNote that there are $\dbinom{n}{8}$ numbers of $n$ digits or less with binary representation having $8$ ones, because there are $8$ places to put the ones. Since $\dbinom{12}{8} = 495$ and $\dbinom{13}{8} = 1287$ , we know that $N$ has $13$ digits. Because the $496$ th number in S is the first 13 digit number in S, we are looking for the $1000 - 496 + 1 = 505$ th 13th digit number in S. Consider $13$ digit slots forming the binary number $N$ . The first slot must contain a $1$ , because $N$ has $13$ digits. Now, we have $7$ remaining ones and $5$ zeros. Among the thirteen digit numbers in S, the ones with second digit $0$ come first. Since we have $7$ ones and $4$ zeros at this point, there are $\dbinom{11}{4} = 330$ of these. Now we are looking for the $505 - 330 = 175$ th 13 digit number in S starting with two ones. However, there are $\dbinom{10}{4} = 210$ 13 digit numbers in S starting with "110", so we know that $N$ starts with $110$ . There are $\dbinom{9}{3} = 84$ 13 digit numbers in S starting with "1100", so N in the $175 - 84 = 91$ th 13 digit number in S starting with 1101. There are $\dbinom{8}{3} = 56$ 13 digit numbers in S starting with 11010, so N is the 35th 13 digit number in S starting with 11011. There are $\dbinom{7}{3} = 35$ 13 digit numbers in S starting with 110110, so $N$ is the last of these, or the greatest, which is $1101101111000$ , which in decimal is $7032$ , so our answer is $\boxed{032}$

<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>This sequence has all the numbers with 8 ones and 0 zeroes, followed by all the numbers with 8 ones and 1 zero, and so on. (in that order) There are  $\binom{7+k}{7}$  integers with k zeroes, so there are  $\binom{8+k}{8}$  integers with less than or equal to k zeroes, by the Hockey Stick Identity. Thus the 1000th number in the sequence is the  $1000-\binom{12}{8}=505^{\text{th}}$  number with 8 ones and 5 zeroes, so 13 digits in base 2.
Now we consider whether each digit in base 2 is a 0 or a 1. We do this by checking how many numbers have a 0 in the next place and satisfy the property. If this is (strictly) less than our current counter, we subtract i.
Example: There are 330 numbers with the first 2 digits  $10$ , thus we want the  $505-330=175^{\text{th}}$  number beginning with  $11$ . Because there are 210 numbers beginning with 110, our third digit is 0. Continuing in this manner, we have  $N=1101101111000_2=7032$ , so our answer is  $\fbox{032}$ .</details>

Subtract the two equations to give us  $(a-b)+\frac{20d-20c}{|w|^2}=4$ .  Subtract the other two equations to give  $(d-c)+\frac{12a-12b}{|z|^2}=14$ .  Let  $a-b=m, d-c=n, |w|^2=o$  and  $|z^2|=p$ .  This gives us:   $m+\frac{20n}{o}=4$  and  $n+\frac{12m}{p}=14$ .  We desire to find  $op$ .  To do so, multiply the first equation by  $\frac{12}{p}$  to give us  $\frac{12m}{p}+\frac{240m}{op}=\frac{48}{p}$  and  $n+\frac{12m}{p}=14$ .  Subtract the two equations to give us:   $n-\frac{240m}{op}=14-\frac{48}{p}$ .  Assume that  $n=14$  and  $\frac{240m}{o}=48$  or  $5m=o$  which is a possible solution for this equation.  From  $n=14$ , we get  $12(a-b)=0$  or  $a=b$ .  From this, we get  $\frac{20d-20c}{|w|^2}=4$  or  $\frac{20*14}{|w|^2}=4\implies |w|^2=70$ .  We now find that from our equation  $a+\frac{20d}{|w|^2}=5$  and  $b+\frac{20c}{|w|^2}=1$ , that we get  $a+\frac{2(14-c)}{7}=5$  and  $a+\frac{2c}{7}=1$ .  Therefore we have  $2a+4=6$  or  $a=1$ .  Therefore  $|z^2|=(\sqrt{a^2+a^2})^2=2$ , and we have  $|zw|^2=|z|^2*|w|^2=70*2=\boxed{140}$ .</details>

stem_md: Let  $x$  and  $y$  be real numbers such that  $\frac{\sin{x}}{\sin{y}} = 3$  and  $\frac{\cos{x}}{\cos{y}} = \frac{1}{2}$ . The value of  $\frac{\sin{2x}}{\sin{2y}} + \frac{\cos{2x}}{\cos{2y}}$  can be expressed in the form  $\frac{p}{q}$ , where  $p$  and  $q$  are relatively prime positive integers. Find  $p + q$ .
solution_md: <details><summary>Lol why is this a number 9</summary>From the first equation we have  $\sin x=3\sin y$  and  $2\cos x=\cos y$ .  We know that  $\frac{\sin 2x}{\sin 2y}=\frac{\sin x\cos x}{\sin y \cos y}=\frac32$  and  $\frac{\cos 2x}{\cos 2y}$  is equal to  $\frac{2\cos^2(x)-1}{2\cos^2(y)-1}$ .  We know note that we have  $\cos x=\frac{\cos y}{2}$  therefore squaring both of the equations  $\sin x=3\sin y$  and  $\cos x=\frac{\cos y}{2}$  gives us  $1=9\sin^2 y+\frac{\cos^2 y}{4}$ .  Use the equation  $9\sin^2 y+9\cos^2 y=9$  to give us  $8=\frac{35}{4}\cos^2(y)$  or  $\cos^2(y)=\frac{32}{35}$ .  From this, we know that also  $4\cos^2 x=\cos^2 y$  or  $\cos^2 x=\frac{8}{35}$ .  Therefore, substitute this back into  $\frac{2*\frac{8}{35}-1}{2*\frac{32}{35}-1}$ .  Therefore  $\frac{\cos 2x}{\cos 2y}$  is equal to  $\frac{16-35}{64-35}=\frac{-19}{29}$ .  Therefore we need to find  $\frac32-\frac{19}{29}$  to give us  $\frac{87}{58}-\frac{38}{58}=\frac{49}{58}$ .  Therefore the answer is  $49+58=\boxed{107}$ .</details>

SolutionWe know that $\dfrac{\sin{2x}}{\sin{2y}} = \dfrac{2\sin{x}\cos{x}}{2\sin{y}\cos{y}} = 3 \cdot \dfrac12 = \dfrac{3}{2}$ We also know that $\sin^2{x} = 9\sin^2{y}$ and $1-\sin^2{y} = 4(1-\sin^2{x})$ , so $4(1 - 9\sin^2{y})= 1 - \sin^2{y}$ , and $3 = 35\sin^2{y}$ , so $\dfrac{3}{35} = \sin^2{y}$ and $\dfrac{27}{35} = \sin^2{x}$ So \begin{eqnarray*} \frac{\sin{2x}}{\sin{2y}} + \frac{\cos{2x}}{\cos{2y}} &=& \dfrac{3}{2} + \dfrac{1 - 2\sin^2{x}}{1 - \sin^2{y}} &=& \dfrac32 + \dfrac{1-54/35}{1-6/35} &=& \dfrac32 - \dfrac{19}{29} &=& \dfrac{49}{58} \end{eqnarray*} and the answer is $49 + 58 = \boxed{107}$

stem_md: Find the number of positive integers  $n$  less than  $1000$  for which there exists a positive real number  $x$  such that  $n = x \lfloor x \rfloor$ . **Note**:  $\lfloor x \rfloor$  is the greatest integer less than or equal to  $x$ .
solution_md:
<details><summary>solution</summary>Let  $\lfloor x\rfloor=a$  and  $\{x\}=a$ , where  $\{x\}$  denotes the fractional part of  $x$ . Then  $x=a+k$ , so  $n=a(a+k)=a^2+ak$  must be an integer. Therefore  $ak$  is an integer, so  $k$  must be rational. Thus there are  $a$  choices for  $k$ :  $\frac{0}{a}$ ,  $\frac{1}{a}$ ,..., $\frac{a-1}{a}$ . Since  $n<1000$ , then  $a\leq 31$ , and even when  $ak$  is maximized, in which case  $ak=30$ ,  $n$  still does not exceed 1000. Therefore for each value of  $a$  between 1 and 31, there are  $a$  integers that work, so the answer is
\[\sum_{a=1}^{31}a=\frac{31\cdot 32}{2}=\boxed{496}.\]</details>

Let  $f_1(x) = \frac{2}{3}-\frac{3}{3x+1}$ , and for  $n \ge 2$ , define  $f_n(x) = f_1(f_{n-1} (x))$ . The value of x that satisfies  $f_{1001}(x) = x - 3$  can be expressed in the form  $\frac{m}{n}$ ,
where  $m$  and  $n$  are relatively prime positive integers. Find  $m + n$ .
solution_md:
Let $f_1(x) = \frac{2}{3}-\frac{3}{3x+1}$ , and for $n \ge 2$ , define $f_n(x) = f_1(f_{n-1} (x))$ . The value of x that satisfies $f_{1001}(x) = x - 3$ can be expressed in the form $\frac{m}{n}$ , where $m$ and $n$ are relatively prime positive integers. Find $m + n$ .
Solution$f_1(x) = \dfrac23 - \dfrac3{3x+1}$ $f_2(x) = \dfrac23 - \dfrac3{3\left(\dfrac23 - \dfrac3{3x+1}\right) + 1} = \dfrac23 - \dfrac{3}{3 - \dfrac{9}{3x+1}} = \dfrac23 - \dfrac{1}{1 - \dfrac3{3x+1}} = \dfrac23 - \dfrac{3x+1}{3x-2} = -\dfrac13 - \dfrac{3}{3x-2}$ $f_3(x) = \dfrac23 - \dfrac3{3\left(-\dfrac13 - \dfrac{3}{3x-2}\right) + 1} = \dfrac23 - \dfrac{3}{- \dfrac{9}{3x-2}} = \dfrac23+\dfrac{3x-2}{3}$ $f_4(x) = \dfrac23 - \dfrac3{3\left(\dfrac23+\dfrac{3x-2}{3}\right)+1} = \dfrac23 - \dfrac{3}{3+(3x-2)} = \dfrac23 - \dfrac{3}{3x+1} = f_1(x)$ Therefore, $f_{1001}(x) = f_2(x) = -\dfrac13 - \dfrac{3}{3x-2} = x-3$ , so $2-3x - 9 = 9x^2-33x+18$ , so $9x^2 - 30x +25 = 0 \implies 3x-5 = 0 \implies x = \dfrac{5}{3}$ So the answer is $\boxed{008}$

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%B6bius_transformation

with associated matrix  $$ A = \begin{bmatrix}
    (1-q) & (q-q^2-1)  
   1 & q 
\end{bmatrix} $$  The eigenvalues  $\lambda_1,\lambda_2$  satisfy its characteristics equation   $$ \text{det}(A-\lambda I) = \text{det} \begin{bmatrix}
    (1-q)-\lambda & (q-q^2-1)  
   1 & q -\lambda

which simplifies to  $$ \lambda^2 - \lambda+1=0 $$  Note that  $\lambda^3+1 = (\lambda+1)(\lambda^2-\lambda+1) = 0$ .

As a rule of thumb, on the amc 10/12 and aime, if they give you a problem involving a sequence of something (in this case functions), you should always list out the fist few terms of the sequence and then pray that something good happens (typically a repeat in the sequence). In this case, we get  $f_3(x) = x$  by algebra, and the problem basically unfolds from there.

Note that:  $$ f_1(x)=\frac{6x-7}{9x+3} $$    $$ f_2(x)=\frac{3x+7}{-9x+6} $$    $$ f_3(x)=x $$  so  $$ \frac{3x+7}{-9x+6}=f_2(x)=f_{1001}(x)=x-3. $$  Solving gives:  $$ 3x+7=(x-3)(6-9x)=-9x^2+33x-18\Rightarrow 9x^2-30x+25=0\Rightarrow x=\frac53\Rightarrow\boxed{008}. $$

solution_md: **Proposed problem.** Let $S_k$ be the sum of the first $k$ terms of the arithmetic sequence $a_1\ ,\ a_2\,\ a_3\ \ldots .$ Show that the value of the expression $\frac{S_m}{m}\cdot (n-p) + \frac{S_n}{n}\cdot (p-m) +\ \frac{S_p}{p}\cdot (m-n)$ does not depend on the numbers $m\ ,\ n\ ,\ p$ nor on the choice of the arithmetic sequence.**Proof.** $\frac {a_m-a_n}{m-n}=\frac {a_n-a_p}{n-p}=\frac {a_p-a_m}{p-m}=r\implies$ $\boxed {p\left(a_m-a_n\right)+m\left(a_n-a_p\right)+n\left(a_p-a_m\right)=0}\ (*)\implies$ $\boxed {\ (p-n)\cdot a_m+(m-p)\cdot a_n+(n-m)\cdot a_p=0\ }$ - first **invariant** . Since $\frac {S_m}{m}=\frac{a_1+a_m}{2}$ a.s.o. obtain that $\frac {\frac {S_m}{m}-\frac {S_n}{n}}{a_m-a_n}=\frac {\frac {S_n}{n}-\frac {S_p}{p}}{a_n-a_p}=\frac {\frac {S_p}{p}-\frac {S_m}{m}}{a_p-a_m}=\frac 12\stackrel{(*)}{\implies}$ $p\cdot\left(\frac {S_m}{m}-\frac {S_n}{n}\right)+$ $m\cdot\left(\frac {S_n}{n}-\frac {S_p}{p}\right)+$ $n\cdot \left(\frac {S_p}{p}-\frac {S_m}{m}\right)=0\implies$ $\boxed {\ (p-n)\cdot \frac {S_m}{m}+(m-p)\cdot\frac {S_n}{n}+(n-m)\cdot\frac {S_p}{p}=0\ }$ - second **invariant** .

stem_md: Find the greatest value of the expression \[ \frac{1}{x^2-4x+9}+\frac{1}{y^2-4y+9}+\frac{1}{z^2-4z+9} \] where  $x$ ,  $y$ ,  $z$  are nonnegative real numbers such that  $x+y+z=1$ .
solution_md:
My solution:
let  $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{x^2-4x+9}$ .
By finding second derivate, we can see that  $f(x)$  on  $[0,1]$  is convex.
Applying Petrovic's inequality we have: $f(x)+f(y)+f(z)\leq f(x+y+z) + (3-1)\cdot f(0)$ .
So, the expression is greater or equal than  $f(1)+2f(0)=\dfrac{7}{18}$ Checking with  $0,0,1$  we can see that this value can be satisfied.

stem_md:
It is given the equation  $x^4-2ax^3+a(a+1)x^2-2ax+a^2=0$ .
a) Find the greatest value of  $a$ , such that this equation has at least one real root.
b) Find all the values of  $a$ , such that the equation has at least one real root.
solution_md: I'd say the main motivation are those factors  $2$ . One of the main ways to discover apparently impossible factorisations is to look for perfect squares and add/subtract lacking terms, adjusting what is left. In this case, the factors "2" remind us about the square of sum. Observing the expression  $-2ax^3$ , plus the fact there's just  $x^4$  with higher degree, we try  $(x^2 - ax)^2 = (x^2)^2 - 2(x^2)(ax) + (ax)^2$ . Thus,  $x^4 - 2ax^3 + a(a + 1)x^2 - 2ax + a^2 = (x^2 - ax)^2 + ax^2 - 2ax + a^2 = x^2(x - a)^2 + ax^2 - 2ax + a^2$ . Now, observing the expression  $-2ax$ , plus the fact there's just  $a^2$  with lower degree, we try  $(x - a)^2 = x^2 - 2ax + a^2$ . Thus,  $x^2(x - a)^2 + ax^2 - 2ax + a^2 = x^2(x - a)^2 + (a - 1)x^2 + (x - a)^2 = (x^2 + 1)(x - a)^2 + (a - 1)x^2$ . Finally,  $x^4 - 2ax^3 + a(a + 1)x^2 - 2ax + a^2 = 0 <=> (x^2 + 1)(x - a)^2 + (a - 1)x^2 = 0 <=> (x^2 + 1)(x - a)^2 = (1 - a)x^2$ .

Find all couples of natural numbers  $(a,b)$  not relatively prime ( $\gcd(a,b)\neq\ 1$ ) such that
\[\gcd(a,b)+9\operatorname{lcm}[a,b]+9(a+b)=7ab.\]
solution_md:
Here is my solution 
Let  $d=gcd(a,b)$ ,  $a=dx$  , $b=dy$ Now  $lcm[a,b]=dxy$  the relation becomes  $$ 1+9xy+9(x+y)=7dxy. $$    $$ \implies \frac{1}{xy}+9+\frac{9}{y}+\frac{9}{x}=7d $$  Now  $x, y\geq 1$  and x and y are integers  so  $l. H. S\leq 28$ .hence 
We get  $d\leq 4$  $case 1:d=4$ The solution is obvious as  $(x, y) =(1,1)$  $case 2:d=3$ If  $x, y\geq 2$  we get   $$ \frac{1}{4}+9+\frac{9}{2}+\frac{9}{2}\leq 19 $$  So only case left is when  $(x, y) =1,2$ But this gives value greater than 21.hence no solutions  $case 3:d=2$ If  $x\geq 3$ , $y\geq5$ then we get   $$ \frac{1}{15}+9+\frac{9}{3}+\frac{9}{5}< 14 $$  So we have to check cases when  $x\leq 3$ ,  $y\leq 5$ So easy bash gives solutions as  $(x, y) =(2,19)$  $case 4:d=1$ Not possible as  $\frac{1}{xy}+9+\frac{9}{y}+\frac{9}{x} >9$ .
So all solutions are  $(a, b) =(4,4),(38,4)$  and it's permutations.

stem_md: Initially there are  $n+1$  monomials on the blackboard:  $1,x,x^2, \ldots, x^n $ . Every minute each of  $k$  boys simultaneously write on the blackboard the sum of some two polynomials that were written before. After  $m$  minutes among others there are the polynomials  $S_1=1+x,S_2=1+x+x^2,S_3=1+x+x^2+x^3,\ldots ,S_n=1+x+x^2+ \ldots +x^n$  on the blackboard. Prove that  $ m\geq \frac{2n}{k+1} $ .
solution_md: **Lemma.** Suppose $\{a_1\},\{a_2\},...,\{a_n\}$ are singletons sets written on a board. Meanwhile, in each minute, we replace two existing sets with their union. Then we arrived at the set $\{a_1,...,a_n\}$ after $n-1$ minutes regardless of how we act. Proof. In each step the number of sets decrease by $1$ . Hence the number of sets must be $1$ after $n-1$ minutes. $\blacksquare$ In the following we view each polynoial as the set of monomials that sum to it (for example $1+x^3+x^5$ will be considered as $\{1,x^3,x^5\}$ ) Now we return to the original problem. Notice that the polynomial $P_0=S_n=1+x+...+x^n$ finally appeared on the blackboard. It must be the sum of two polynomials $P_1$ and $Q_1$ where $P_1,Q_1$ exists before $P_0$ , $P_1$ contains the monomial $1$ while $Q_1$ does not. Similarly, $P_1$ can be expressed as the sum of two pre-existed polynomials $P_2$ and $Q_2$ where the monomial $1$ belongs to $P_2$ but not $Q_2$ . Define $P_3,...$ similarly. Now suppose the sequence ends at $P_x$ , then $$ \{1\}=P_x\subset P_{x-1}\subset ...\subset P_1\subset P_0=\{1,...,x^n\} $$ Meanwhile, $|Q_i|=|P_{i}|-|P_{i+1}|$ , hence $$ \sum_{i=1}^{x}|Q_i|=\sum_{i=1}|P_{i}|-|P_{i+1}|=|P_0|-|P_x|=n $$ We say that a polynomial $A$ is the preproduct of $B$ if $A$ is not a monomial and $B$ is obtained by adding $A$ with some other polynomials. Then notice that all $Q_i$ 's are disjoint and hence their preproduct are different. Meanwhile, by the lemma the total number of preproduct of $Q_1,...,Q_x$ is $$ \left(\sum_{i=1}^x|Q_i|\right)-x\geq n-m $$ where we use the obvious bound $x\leq m$ . Now notice that there are only $mk$ new polynomials other than $1,x,...,x^n$ . Among them, there are $S_1,...,S_n$ and the $n-m$ preproducts of $Q_1,...,Q_x$ . Therefore, $$ 2n-m\leq mk $$ which implies $m\geq \frac{2n}{k+1}$ as desired.

*Proof:* For  $n=1$  the claim is easily observed to be true.

Take any vertex of degree three that is adjacent to two leaf nodes. Remove the leaf nodes and we have a graph with  $n$  leaf nodes. So there are  $2(n-1)$  vertices by induction. Prove that  $k^2\ge 25/3$ .

Then, all the white squares are coloured red and blue such that any two initially white squares that share a corner are different colours. (One is red and the other is blue.) For every line segment  $I$  that is parallel to  $\ell$ , we can count the difference between the length of its red and its blue areas. Prove that for every such line  $\ell$  there exists a number  $C$  that exceeds all those differences that we can calculate.
solution_md:
We color the black squares alternating green and yellow, such that greens are to the right of reds, and yellows to the right of blues.

For any line segment, let  $B$  be the amount of its length in the blue region, and similar for the others.  Clearly,  $B+G-R-Y$  and  $B+Y-R-G$  are bounded because they are the differences along  $B$  of the lengths in alternating columns, rows, respectively.  Hence their sum,  $2(B-R)$ , is bounded, and  $B-R$  is bounded as desired.

Given is the polynomial  $P(x)$  and the numbers  $a_1,a_2,a_3,b_1,b_2,b_3$  such that  $a_1a_2a_3\not=0$ . Suppose that for every  $x$ , we have
\[P(a_1x+b_1)+P(a_2x+b_2)=P(a_3x+b_3)\]
Prove that the polynomial  $P(x)$  has at least one real root.
solution_md:
Given is the polynomial $P(x)$ and the numbers $a_1,a_2,a_3,b_1,b_2,b_3$ such that $a_1a_2a_3\not=0$ . Suppose that for every $x$ , we have \[P(a_1x+b_1)+P(a_2x+b_2)=P(a_3x+b_3)\] Prove that the polynomial $P(x)$ has at least one real root.
Let's $P(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{n}c_ix^i$ , $c_n \ne 0$ , $n \in \mathbb{N}$ . Since $c_n(a_jx+b_j)^n=c_na_j^nx^n+...$ then equating the coefficients of $x^n$ in the original equation we get: $a_1^n+a_2^n=a_3^n$ . If $a_1=a_2=a_3=a$ then $2a^n=a^n$ and $a=0$ - a contradiction. So $a_1 \ne a_3$ or $a_2 \ne a_3$ . WLOG $a_2 \ne a_3$ . For $x=\frac{b_3-b_2}{a_2-a_3}$ we have: $a_2x+b_2=a_3x+b_3 \implies P(a_2x+b_2)=P(a_3x+b_3) \implies P(a_1x+b_1)=0$ . Thus $x=\frac{a_1b_3-a_1b_2+a_2b_1-a_3b_1}{a_2-a_3}$ is the root of $P$ .

stem_md:
On a circle there are  $2n+1$  points, dividing it into equal arcs ( $n\ge 2$ ). Two players take turns to erase one point. If after one player's turn, it turned out that all the triangles formed by the remaining points on the circle were obtuse, then the player wins and the game ends.
Who has a winning strategy: the starting player or his opponent?
solution_md:
Here is a solution in the spirit of the above, but with different execution. Very nice problem :)

Consider the  $2n+1$  collections of  $n$  contiguous points  $A_1, \ldots, A_{2n+1}$  (indices mod  $2n+1$ ). The game proceeds as follows: In a move, one picks an integer  $k$  and decrements  $S_k, S_{k+1}, \ldots, S_{k+n}$ , where  $S_k$  is defined as  $|A_k|$ . A player wins when some  $S_i$  becomes zero. Another restriction we impose is that no integer  $k$  can be picked twice.

This allows for the following transformation: Given  $2n+1$  piles of stones, each consisting of  $n$  stones, a move consists of picking  $n$  consecutive piles that have not been chosen before and removing a stone from each of the piles. The win condition is to fully deplete a condition; equivalently, the first player to make a pile have  $1$  stone loses, since the other player now just picks the last block of  $n$  piles that contains the pile with  $1$  stone left and wins. Thus we play the game where the player to make a pile have exactly  $1$  stone loses.

Now, we claim that the **second player** always wins. For a block  $P_1\dots P_n$  of stones, we say that the piles  $P_0$  and  $P_{n+1}$  are the two *pivots* of the block. Also, note that each pile is the pivot of two blocks. Thus, we may represent the situation as a graph  $G$  in which blocks are vertices and piles are edges. Since  $(n,2n+1) = 1$ ,  $G$  is a  $C_{2n+1}$ , and players alternate turns picking vertices. Note that at any point, the vertices chosen form a bunch of disjoint paths. We claim that second player can always ensure that after their turn, each path has even length. We induct on the number of turns; after 0 this is clear. Now once first player moves, one path has odd length, and so second player just picks a vertex so as to extend the odd path (it's fine if this merges with another path, since we just add an even number of edges on to the now-even path).

To see why this wins, note that after  $2m$  vertices have been chosen, they can be partitioned into  $m$  edges. Thus if we call the pivots  $Q_1, \ldots, Q_m$ , we see that we have removed  $m$  stones from each pile but  $m-1$  from  $Q_1, \ldots, Q_m$ . This results, when  $m = n-2$ , into us having  $n-2$  piles with  $3$  stones each, and  $n+3$  piles of  $2$  stones each. It is clear that first player's next move must remove a stone from one of the piles with  $2$  stones, so first player must lose.  $\blacksquare$

stem_md: For a positive integer  $n$  define  $S_n=1!+2!+\ldots +n!$ . Prove that there exists an integer  $n$  such that  $S_n$  has a prime divisor greater than  $10^{2012}$ .
solution_md:
Call a prime  $p$  *special* if, for any  $\alpha\geq0$ , the set  $\{n:p^\alpha\mid S_n\}$  is infinite. **Claim 1.** If  $p$  is special, then  $p\mid S_{p-1}$ .

*Proof.* For  $n\geq p$ , we have  $S_n\equiv S_{p-1}\pmod p$ , and the result follows.  $\square$ **Claim 2.** If  $p$  is special and  $p$  divides  $n$ , then  $v_p(S_n)>v_p(n!)$ .

*Proof.* We observe that  $S_{n+p-1}-S_n=n!\cdot T$ , where  $$ T=(n+1)+(n+1)(n+2)+\cdots+(n+1)(n+2)\cdots(n+p-1)\text{.} $$  Since  $p\mid n$ , we have  $T\equiv S_{p-1}\equiv0\pmod{p}$ , by Claim 1. Therefore,  $v_p(S_{n+p-1}-S_n)>v_p(n!)$ .

On the other hand, for any  $k\geq n+p$ , one has  $v_p(k!)>v_p(n!)$ , which implies that  $S_m\equiv S_{n+p-1}\pmod{p^{v_p(n!)+1}}$  for every  $m\geq n+p$ . Since  $p$  is special, it follows that  $p^{v_p(n!)+1}\mid S_{n+p-1}$ , i.e.  $v_p(S_{n+p-1})>v_p(n!)$ .

It follows that  $$ v_p(S_n)=v_p(S_{n+p-1}-(S_{n+p-1}-S_n))\geq\min\{v_p(S_{n+p-1}),v_p(S_{n+p-1}-S_n)\}>v_p(n!)\text{,} $$  as desired.  $\square$ **Claim 3.** If  $p$  is special and  $n\equiv -1\pmod{p}$ , then  $v_p(S_n)=v_p((n+1)!)$ .

*Proof.* By Claim 2, we have  $v_p(S_{n+1})>v_p((n+1)!)$ . Hence  $v_p(S_n)=v_p(S_{n+1}-(n+1)!)=v_p((n+1)!)$ .  $\square$ Assume now FTSOC that the desired conclusion does not hold. Let  $M=10^{2012}$ . Let  $q$  be any prime larger than  $M$ . Let  $$ n=k\prod_{p\text{ special}}p-1 $$  where  $k$  is a sufficiently large integer, not divisible by any special prime, to be chosen later (note that by assumption any special prime is smaller than  $M$ , hence the product above is finite).

By definition of special, together with the assumption that  $S_n$  is not divisible by any prime larger than  $M$ , the powers of non-special primes appearing in the prime factorization of  $S_n$  are bounded by an absolute constant independent of  $k$ . Hence we have  $$ S_n\leq C\prod_{p\text{ special}}p^{v_p((n+1)!)} $$  for some absolute constant  $C$ . By our assumption on  $k$ , if  $p$  is special then  $v_p((n+1)!)=v_p(n!)+1$ , hence, by taking  $C'=C\prod_{p\text{ special}}p$ , we find that there exists an absolute constant  $C'$  such that  $$ S_n\leq C'\prod_{p\text{ special}}p^{v_p(n!)}\text{.} $$  On the other hand, we have  $$ S_n\geq n!\geq q^{v_q(n!)}\prod_{p\text{ special}}p^{v_p(n!)}\text{.} $$  Comparing the two inequalities, it follows that  $q^{v_q(n!)}\leq C'$ . This is clearly false if  $k$  is sufficiently large.**Note:** The natural guess here would be that no prime is special, which trivializes the problem. In fancy language, the statement that  $p$  is not special seems to be equivalent to the statement that the infinite series  $$ \sum_{k=0}^\infty k! $$  does *not* converge to  $0$  in the  $p$ -adic numbers  $\mathbb{Q}_p$ .

I have not been able to prove this, forcing me to contend with the existence of special primes as in the solution above. A quick Google search seems to reveal that this  $p$ -adic non-vanishing result is indeed known; it seems to be an open problem whether the sum of the above series in  $\mathbb{Q}_p$  is irrational for every prime  $p$ .

Suppose that the prime divisors of  $S_n$  are always at most  $10^{2012}$ . By Stirling, we have the crucial approximation  $\ln n! \sim n\log n \implies \log S_n=\Omega(n \log n)$ . This means that for all sufficiently large  $n$ , there must exist some prime  $p\leq 10^{2012}$  (possibly depending on  $n$ ) such that  $\nu_p(S_n) \geq n\sqrt{\log n}$ , otherwise  $$ S_n \leq \left(\prod_{p \leq 10^{2012}} p\right)^{n \sqrt{\log n}} \implies \log S_n=O(n \sqrt{\log n}), $$  which is dominated by  $n \log n$  as  $n \to \infty$ : contradiction. For a prime  $p \leq 10^{-2012}$ , call a positive integer  $n$  *$p$ -good* if  $\nu_p(S_n) \geq n\sqrt{\log n}$ . There must be some  $p$  for which the upper density of  $p$ -good integers is at least  $10^{2012}$ , else by union bounding upper densities we get that there should be infinitely many integers which are not  $q$ -good for any prime  $q$ .

For this prime  $p$ , there exist infinitely many pairs of positive integers  $(k,d)$  such that  $k$  and  $k+d$  are both  $p$ -good, and  $0 \leq d \leq 10^{2012}$ . For these pairs, we have  $$ \nu_p(S_{k+d}-S_k) \geq k\sqrt{\log k} \implies (k+1)!+\cdots+(k+d)! \equiv 0 \pmod{p^{k\lfloor \sqrt{\log k}\rfloor}}. $$  In general, by Legendre's formula we have  $\nu_p(k!)\leq 2k$ , so by dividing out we have the congruence  $$ (k+1)+(k+1)(k+2)+\cdots+(k+1)(k+2)\ldots(k+d) \equiv 0 \pmod{p^{k\lfloor \sqrt{\log k}\rfloor-2k}}. $$  Clearly, the LHS is a positive integer, but on the other hand it is also on the order of  $k^d$ , so asymptotically it is  $O(k^{10^{2012}})$ , or polynomial. But for  $k$  large enough, this is dominated by  $p^{k\lfloor \log k\rfloor-2k}$ , which is super-exponential. But for the congruence to hold, we need  $(k+1)+\cdots+(k+1)\ldots(k+d) \geq p^{k\lfloor \sqrt{\log k}\rfloor-2k}$ . This is a contradiction, so we're done.  $\blacksquare$

The answer is  $5 \cdot 503=1509$ . For a construction, label the vertices  $0,\ldots,2011$  in clockwise order, and take vertices  $0,1,\ldots,1005,1006,1008,\ldots,2010$ . Edges  $\overline{ab}$  and  $\overline{cd}$  are parallel iff  $a+b \equiv c+d \pmod{2012}$ . Note that all edges  $\overline{ab}$  where  $a+1=b$  have  $a+b \pmod{2012}$  unique, as with all edges where  $a+2=b$ , which covers all edges. Furthermore, since  $a+b$  is odd in the first case and even in the second, there are no overlaps "between" groups either, as desired.
For the bound, define the *pseudolength* of an edge  $\overline{ab}$ , where  $b$  is clockwise along the polygon from  $a$ , to be  $b-a \pmod{2012}$ , and define the *pseudoperimeter* of a polygon formed from vertices of our  $2012$ -gon in the obvious way. Suppose that we have  $x$  edges of odd pseudolength and  $y$  edges of even pseudolength, so we wish to maximize  $x+y$ . Obviously, the pseudoperimeter of the polygon formed is always  $2012$ , so  $x+2y \leq 2012$ . Furthermore, the pseudolength of an edge  $\overline{ab}$  has the same parity as  $a+b \pmod{2012}$ , so every odd-pseudolength edge must occupy an odd residue class modulo  $2012$ . Since there are  $1006$  of these, we have  $x \leq 1006$ . Hence  $$ x+y=\frac{(x+2y)+x}{2}\leq \frac{2012+1006}{2}=1509 $$  as desired.  $\blacksquare$

Solved with **stillwater_25**. We solve the more general problem for an arbitrary regular $4n-$ gon. We claim that the maximum number of vertices we can pick is $3n$ . Label the vertices $0,1,\dots , 4n-1$ in the clockwise direction. It is known that edges $\overline{ab}$ and $\overline{cd}$ are parallel if and only if $a+b \equiv c+d \pmod{2012}$ . **Construction :**Consider the polygon formed by joining vertices $0,1,2,\dots , 2n , 2n+2 , \dots , 4n-2,0$ . *Proof :* First it is clear that the above set of vertices $\mathcal{V}$ has $3n$ elements. Now, note that the first $2n$ sides (in the first 'half' of our $4n-$ gon) are non-parallel among themselves quite clearly. Similarly the last $n$ sides are also non-parallel among themselves. Also one of the first sides and one of the last sides cannot be parallel. This is because the last sides are of the form $\overline{c(c+2)}$ and the first sides are of the form $\overline{a(a+1)}$ , so \[a+(a+1) = 2a+1 \equiv 1 \not \equiv 0 \equiv 2c +2 = c + (c+2) \pmod{2}\] and since $2\mid 4n$ this implies that they are also distinct $\pmod{4n}$ so the parallel condition is not satisfied. For the bound, starting from vertex $0$ pair the vertices with its neighbors. For example, we pair $0-1$ , $2-3$ , $\dots $ , $4n-1,4n$ . For any pair $P$ let its *antipodal pair* $P'$ denote the pair joining the two vertices diametrically opposite to the points in pair $P$ . Note that if a pair $P \in \mathcal{V}$ it must be a side of our polygon as there are no other vertices between the two vertices in $P$ . Thus, all four vertices in $P$ and $P'$ cannot be in $\mathcal{V}$ since $P\parallel P'$ quite clearly. Thus, out of these 4 points at most 3 can be in our polygon, which summing across all pairs implies that we can have at most $3n$ vertices in $\mathcal{V}$ and we are done.

stem_md: The positive real numbers  $a_1,\ldots ,a_n$  and  $k$  are such that  $a_1+\cdots +a_n=3k$ ,  $a_1^2+\cdots +a_n^2=3k^2$  and  $a_1^3+\cdots +a_n^3>3k^3+k$ . Prove that the difference between some two of  $a_1,\ldots,a_n$  is greater than  $1$ .
solution_md:
Although my solution is too horrible and cannot be as elegant as mahanmath's, but I would like to present another approach to this nice problem
Without the loss of generality, we assume  $a_1>a_2>...>a_n$  and difference between any two numbers is less than 1, hence we have  $a_1-a_n \leq 1$ So, we have  $a_i, a_j, 1$  are sides of a triangle(degenerate triangle is allowed).
We have following lemmas:
Lemma 1:If  $a,b,c$  are sides of a triangle(degenerate triangle is allowed) then  $a^2+b^2+c^2 \leq 2ab+2bc+2ca$ Substitute  $a=x+y, b=y+z, c=z+x$ , we see that  $x,y,z \geq 0 \Rightarrow b+c \geq a$ , hence proved.
Lemma 2:Same condition, we have  $a^3+b^3+c^3 \leq 5abc$ Prove as same as above.

Return to the original problem.
We easily have: $\sum_{sym}a_ia_j = 3k^2$ Then, using lemma 1, we have: $\sum a^2_i+a^2_j+1 \leq 2(a_ia_j+a_i+a_j)$  $\Leftrightarrow (n-1)3k^2 + C_n^2 \leq 6k^2 + 6(n-1)k$  $\Leftrightarrow 6k^2 \geq C_n^2 +3(n-1)$  $\Leftrightarrow 6k^2+9 \geq (n+2)^2$  $\Leftrightarrow 3k > n+2(1)$ Now, using the lemma 2, we have: $\sum a_i^3 + a_j^3 + 1 \leq 5a_ia_j$  $\Leftrightarrow (n-1)(\sum a_i^3) + C_n^2 \leq 15k^2$ Also, using the condition  $\sum a_i^3 > 3k^3+k$ , the inequality now equivalent to: $\Leftrightarrow (n-1)(3k^3+k) + C_n^2 \leq 15k^2$  $\Leftrightarrow 45k^2 \geq (n-1)3k(3k^2+1) + 3C_n^2 > (n-1)(n+2)(3k^2+1) + 3C_n^2$  $\Leftrightarrow 45k^2 \geq (n-1)(n+2)(3k^2+1) + 3C_n^2 > C_n^2(6k^2+5)$ (from  $(1)$ ) $\Leftrightarrow C_n^2 < 10 \Rightarrow n \leq 3$ Now we only have to consider the case  $n=2$  and  $n=3$ For  $n=3$ , we have: $(x^3+y^3+z^3)(x+y+z) > (x^2+y^2+z^2)^2 + x^2+y^2+z^2$  $\Leftrightarrow x^2+y^2+z^2 \leq xy(x-y)^2+yz(y-z)^2+zx(z-x)^2 \leq xy+yz+zx$  $\Leftrightarrow x=y=z$ , contradiction!
For  $n=2$ , we have  $a^2+b^2=ab=3k^2 \Rightarrow a=b=0$  Contradiction!!!
Hence proved.


Comment:Although this solution requires many lemmas, but I think it is more natural than mahanmath's solution :D, but of course, not as beautiful as his.

stem_md: $101$  wise men stand in a circle. Each of them either thinks that the Earth orbits Jupiter or that Jupiter orbits the Earth. Once a minute, all the wise men express their opinion at the same time. Right after that, every wise man who stands between two people with a different opinion from him changes his opinion himself. The rest do not change. Prove that at one point they will all stop changing opinions.
solution_md: For simplicity, let $0$ and $1$ be the people who think that the Earth orbits Jupiter and the people who think that Jupiter orbits the Earth respectively. Now from the condition, if a number is differernt from both of its neighbors, then it changes in the next minute. We define a block of $0$ to be at least $2$ consecutive $0$ s in the circle. Define a block of $1$ analogously. The key observation is CLAIM 1. The numbers in a block of $0$ will never change Proof. This is very simple. Indeed, a number changes if and only if it is different from both of its neighbors. However, each of the $0$ s in the middle of the block has two $0$ s as its neighbors. Therefore it will never change. On the other hand, each of the $0$ s at the side of the block has one $0$ as its neighbors, so it never changes as well. $\blacksquare$ Similarly, the numbers in a block of $1$ will never change. Now since there are $101$ numbers which is an odd number, there must be a block initially. CLAIM 2. Aftere finitely many operations, the numbers can be decomposed into blocks. Proof. It suffices to show that there are no elements which does not belong to a block. We perform the following algorithm: We start with a block, WLOG assume that it is a block of $0$ . Consider the element next to it, then by definition it must be $1$ , for example: $$ 100...0 $$ consider the element next to $1$ , if it is a $1$ , then there is a block of $1$ . If it is a $0$ then in the next minute the $1$ will become $0$ , that is $$ 0100...0\to x000...0 $$ Notice that this algorithm must terminate, and that its final state must be the state in which the numbers can be decomposed into blocks. $\blacksquare$ This completes the proof.

Let the opinions be weighed as bits  $\{0, 1\}$  by a King. Consider the largest alternating string  $...01010...$  and note that it is bordered by bits of some non-alternating strings as  $101$  is odd. Any wise man at the end of this string does not change opinions, whereas all other wise men on this string change their opinions. Evidently, the length of the maximal alternating string strictly decreases at each stage. Note also that the length of a non-alternating string can remain the same or increase. It follows that the process eventually terminates.

Alternatively, assign the weights  $\{0,1\}$  to the two opinions. Let  $T$  be the set of consecutive triples  $x,y,z,$  with  $y$  in between, and for any such triple define  $f(x,y,z):=|x-y|+|y-z|.$  Now, if all the wise men are  $x_1, \cdots x_{101},$  then consider  $$ F(x_1, \cdots, x_{101})=\sum_{(x,y,z) \in T} f(x,y,z) $$  Note that  $F \in \mathbb{N}.$  Hence if we can show that  $F$  always decreases, we are done.
Now note that  $(1,0,1) \mapsto (1,1,1), (1,1,0), (0,1,1)$  or  $(0,1,0).$  In the first  $3$  cases, we find that  $f(x,y,z)$  strictly decreases hence so does  $F.$  
It suffices to check that not all triples map to their "complement." Indeed,  $(1,0,1) \mapsto (0,1,0)$  iff  $(1,0,1)$  is surrounded by two zeros, in which case we find two more triples along the borders of  $(0,1,0,1,0).$  Hence if every triple maps to its complement, we find that every triple is alternating, that is of the form  $(0,1,0)$  or  $(1,0,1).$  But this is not possible since  $101$  is odd, and we are done.  $\square$ **P.S.** The last argument is essentially the same as the one in the solution above. Also,  $F$  is basically twice of the (positive) differences of adjacent numbers, which is a very common monovariant. In our case, it is easy to modify the monovariant, and later in the argument that follows (which is needed), we discover that the monovariant is not even needed and the argument is complete in itself. This motivates the solution above.

$101$ wise men stand in a circle. Each of them either thinks that the Earth orbits Jupiter or that Jupiter orbits the Earth. Once a minute, all the wise men express their opinion at the same time. Right after that, every wise man who stands between two people with a different opinion from him changes his opinion himself. The rest do not change. Prove that at one point they will all stop changing opinions.
Call a wise man pro if he doesn't change his opinion (& noob otherwise). Since there are odd no. of wise man, therefore pro exist. Note that a pro will never become noob (since he is adjacent to a man with similar opinion, they both will remain pro). Also note that the no. of noobs is a strict monovariant (since any noob adjacent to a pro will change his opinion and both will have the same opinion , hence the noob will become pro). Since there are only finite no. of wise man, the process terminates when all the wise man become pro.

stem_md: Initially, ten consecutive natural numbers are written on the board. In one turn, you may pick any two numbers from the board (call them  $a$  and  $b$ ) and replace them with the numbers  $a^2-2011b^2$  and  $ab$ . After several turns, there were no initial numbers left on the board. Could there, at this point, be again, ten consecutive natural numbers?
solution_md: the answer is no. assume the contrary.first notice that with this operation the number of even numbers never decrease.if we sometime choose two of odd numbers then the number of even numbers will increase.but at the end we must to have 5 even numbers same as when we start.so we cannot choose two odd numbers simultaneously.because we must to choose every number at least one time then suppose that we choose one of odd numbers at this moment.let it to be  $a$  and  $b$  must be even then  $a^{2}-2011b^{2}\equiv 1(mod 4)$  if we choose odd number instead of  $b$  and even number instead of  $a$  then again we have  $a^{2}-2011b^{2}\equiv 1(mod 4)$  then choosing every odd number will give us a number in the form  $4k+1$  then at the end we must to have at least  $5$  numbers in the form  $4k+1$  but we can have at most  $3$  of them so this is contradiction.
